{{Short description|Metric space with double measurement}}
[[File:7 disks cover 2x disk.svg|thumb|In the [[Euclidean plane]], seven disks of radius {{math|''r''/2}} can cover any disk of radius {{mvar|r}}, so the plane is a doubling space with doubling constant 7 and doubling dimension log<sub>2</sub> 7.]]
In [[mathematics]], a [[metric space]] {{Mvar|X}} with metric {{Mvar|d}} is said to be '''doubling''' if there is some doubling constant {{Math|''M'' > 0}} such that for any {{Math|''x'' &isin; ''X''}} and {{Math|''r'' > 0}}, it is possible to cover the ball {{Math|1=''B''(''x'', ''r'') = {''y'' {{!}} ''d''(''x'', ''y'') < ''r''<nowiki>}</nowiki>}} with the union of at most {{Mvar|M}} balls of radius {{Math|{{sfrac|''r''|2}}}}.<ref>{{cite book| last = Heinonen| first = Juha | title = Lectures on Analysis on Metric Spaces | series = Universitext | publisher = Springer-Verlag | location = New York | year = 2001 | pages = x+140 | isbn = 0-387-95104-0}}</ref> The base-2 [[logarithm]] of {{Mvar|M}} is called the '''doubling dimension''' of {{Mvar|X}}.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Gupta |first1=A. |last2=Krauthgamer |first2=R. |last3=Lee |first3=J.R. |title=44th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, 2003. Proceedings. |chapter=Bounded geometries, fractals, and low-distortion embeddings |date=2003 |chapter-url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1238226 |pages=534–543 |doi=10.1109/SFCS.2003.1238226|isbn=0-7695-2040-5 |s2cid=796386 |url=https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/6603941 }}</ref> [[Euclidean space]]s <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> equipped with the usual Euclidean metric are examples of doubling spaces where the doubling constant {{Mvar|M}} depends on the dimension&nbsp;{{Mvar|d}}. For example, in one dimension, {{Math|1=''M'' = 3}}; and in two dimensions, {{Math|1=''M'' = 7}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/DiskCoveringProblem.html|title=Disk Covering Problem|last=W.|first=Weisstein, Eric|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en|access-date=2018-03-03}}</ref> In general, Euclidean space <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math>  has doubling dimension <math>\Theta(d)</math>.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Zhou |first=Felix |date=21 Feb 2023 |title=Doubling Dimension and Treewidth |url=https://student.cs.uwaterloo.ca/~cfzhou/projects/doubling_dim.pdf}}</ref>

==Assouad's embedding theorem==

An important question in metric space geometry is to characterize those metric spaces that can be embedded in some Euclidean space by a [[Lipschitz continuity|bi-Lipschitz]] function. This means that one can essentially think of the metric space as a subset of Euclidean space. Not all metric spaces may be embedded in Euclidean space. Doubling metric spaces, on the other hand, would seem like they have more of a chance, since the doubling condition says, in a way, that the metric space is not infinite dimensional. However, this is still not the case in general. The [[Heisenberg group]] with its [[Carnot-Carathéodory metric]] is an example of a doubling metric space which cannot be embedded in any Euclidean space.<ref>{{cite journal| last = Pansu| first= Pierre | title = Métriques de Carnot-Carathéodory et quasiisométries des espaces symétriques de rang un| journal = Ann. of Math. |series = Series 2| volume = 129 | year = 1989 | number = 1 | pages = 1–60 | doi=10.2307/1971484| jstor= 1971484 }}</ref>

'''Assouad's Theorem''' states that, for a {{mvar|M}}-doubling metric space {{mvar|X}}, if we give it the metric {{math|''d''(''x'', ''y'')<sup>''ε''</sup>}} for some {{math|0 < ''ε'' < 1}}, then there is a {{mvar|L}}-bi-Lipschitz map <math>f:X \rarr \mathbb{R}^d</math>, where {{mvar|d}} and {{mvar|L}} depend on {{mvar|M}} and {{mvar|ε}}.

==Doubling Measures==

===Definition===
A nontrivial [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] on a metric space ''X'' is said to be '''doubling''' if the measure of any ball is finite and approximately the measure of its double, or more precisely, if there is a constant ''C''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 such that

:<math> 0<\mu(B(x,2r))\leq C\mu(B(x,r))<\infty \, </math>

for all ''x'' in ''X'' and ''r''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0. In this case, we say ''μ'' is '''C-doubling'''. In fact, it can be proved that, necessarily, ''C''&nbsp;<math>\geq</math>&nbsp;2.<ref>{{cite journal| last1 = Soria | last2 = Tradacete | first1 = Javier | first2 = Pedro | title = The least doubling constant of a metric measure space | journal =  Ann. Acad. Sci. Fenn. Math. | volume = 44 | year = 2019  | issue = 2 | pages = 1015–1030 | doi = 10.5186/aasfm.2019.4457 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

A metric measure space that supports a doubling measure is necessarily a doubling metric space, where the doubling constant depends on the constant&nbsp;''C''.  Conversely, every [[complete metric space|complete]] doubling metric space supports a doubling measure.<ref>{{cite journal| last1 = Luukainen | last2 = Saksman | first1 = Jouni | first2 = Eero | title = Every complete doubling metric space carries a doubling measure | journal = Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. | volume = 126 | year = 1998 | number = 2 | pages = 531–534 | doi = 10.1090/s0002-9939-98-04201-4 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jouni|first=Luukkainen|date=1998|title=ASSOUAD DIMENSION: ANTIFRACTAL METRIZATION, POROUS SETS, AND HOMOGENEOUS MEASURES|url=http://www.koreascience.or.kr/article/ArticleFullRecord.jsp?cn=DBSHBB_1998_v35n1_23|journal=Journal of the Korean Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=35|issue=1|issn=0304-9914}}</ref>

===Examples===

A simple example of a doubling measure is [[Lebesgue measure]] on a Euclidean space. One can, however, have doubling measures on Euclidean space that are  [[Singular measures|singular]] with respect to Lebesgue measure. One example on the real line is the [[weak limit]] of the following sequence of measures:<ref>{{cite book| last=Zygmund | first = A. |author-link=Antoni Zygmund | title= Trigonometric Series. Vol. I, II |title-link= Trigonometric Series| series = Cambridge Mathematical Library | edition = Third | publisher = Cambridge University Press | year = 2002 | pages = xii; Vol. I: xiv+383 pp.; Vol. II: viii+364| isbn = 0-521-89053-5}}</ref>

:<math> d\mu_n = \prod_{i=1}^n (1+a\cos (3^i 2\pi x))\,dx,\;\;\; |a|<1.</math>

One can construct another singular doubling measure ''μ'' on the interval [0,&nbsp;1] as follows: for each ''k''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0, partition the [[unit interval]] [0,1] into 3<sup>''k''</sup> intervals of length 3<sup>&minus;''k''</sup>. Let Δ be the collection of all such intervals in [0,1] obtained for each ''k'' (these are the ''triadic intervals''), and for each such interval ''I'', let ''m''(''I'') denote its "middle third" interval. Fix 0&nbsp;<&nbsp;''δ''&nbsp;<&nbsp;1 and let ''μ'' be the measure such that ''μ''([0,&nbsp;1])&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 and for each triadic interval ''I'', ''μ''(''m''(''I''))&nbsp;=&nbsp;''δμ''(''I''). Then this gives a doubling measure on [0,&nbsp;1] singular to Lebesgue measure.<ref>{{cite journal| last = Kahane | first = J.-P. | title = Trois notes sur les ensembles parfaits linéaires| journal = Enseignement Mathémathique |series=Série 2 | volume = 15 | year = 1969 | pages = 185–192}}</ref>

==Applications==

The definition of a doubling measure may seem arbitrary, or purely of geometric interest. However, many results from classical [[harmonic analysis]] and [[computational geometry]] extend to the setting of metric spaces with doubling measures.

== See also ==

* [[Highway dimension]]: this metric parameter generalises the doubling dimension.
